title: Why does crossing the Rubicon mean there's no way back?

post.caption: Ancient Rome, episode 5: Caesar conquers Gaul, the Senate orders him to give up his army, and in January 49 BC he crosses the Rubicon. Alea iacta est. Images: public domain / CC0 (Rubens, Boulanger, Fouquet, Royer, The Met, Rijksmuseum), AI illustration marked. Map data: Natural Earth.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Why does crossing the Rubicon mean there's no way back?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Because of one night in January, 49 BC. Julius Caesar led his army across a small river, and Rome was never the same.
beats.say: Because of one night in January, forty-nine BC. Julius Caesar led his army across a small river, and Rome was never the same.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Is it a big river?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Not at all. It's a small river between Rimini and Cesena, about eighty kilometres long.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Where was Caesar coming from?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Gaul. In eight years, he had conquered what is now France and Belgium. In 52 BC, the Gallic leader Vercingetorix surrendered to him.
beats.say: Gaul. In eight years, he had conquered what is now France and Belgium. In fifty-two BC, the Gallic leader Vercingetorix surrendered to him.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So why was the river a problem?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: It was the border of Italy. A general had to leave his army behind before crossing it. Bringing troops into Italy was treason, punishable by death.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Why not just leave the army?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: His rivals in the Senate, led by Pompey, ordered him to give up his command. Without his army, Caesar expected to be put on trial.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So what did he do?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: He stopped at the river with a single legion, the Thirteenth. Then he gave the order to cross.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Did he say anything?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: According to the historian Suetonius, he said: alea iacta est. The die is cast.
beats.say: According to the historian Suetonius, he said: ah-lay-ah, yak-ta est. The die is cast.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And how did Rome react?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: With panic. Pompey and much of the Senate fled Rome, and then Italy itself.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Did Pompey fight back?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: He did, in Greece. In 48 BC, Caesar crushed him at Pharsalus. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed.
beats.say: He did, in Greece. In forty-eight BC, Caesar crushed him at Pharsalus. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And Caesar?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: He became the master of Rome. His name was now on Roman coins, like this silver denarius.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Is today's Rubicon the real one?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Nobody is completely sure. Rivers here changed course over the centuries. In 1933, Mussolini's government declared the Fiumicino river to be the Rubicon.
beats.say: Nobody is completely sure. Rivers here changed course over the centuries. In nineteen thirty-three, Mussolini's government declared the Fiumicino river to be the Rubicon.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Next time: the Ides of March. Like the video and follow History Sketches so you don't miss it.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And tell us in the comments: what was your Rubicon?
